title: Patience and Delayed Gratification
keyIdea: Patience means waiting for something you want without a big fuss. Waiting can bring something better later, like two biscuits instead of one, as long as the person who made the promise keeps it. Waiting is easier with tricks: put the treat out of sight, keep busy with a song, a toy or counting, and take slow breaths. Staring at it, poking it or asking “Is it time?” again and again make the wait feel longer. While you wait, ask once, kindly. Patience is for things that can wait: if you are hurt, sick or scared, tell a grown-up straight away.
familyTip: Next time your child has to wait, for dinner, a turn or a trip to the park, plan the wait together: “Where shall we put it so we can’t see it? What shall we do until the timer beeps?” Use a kitchen timer or a sand timer so the wait has a clear end, and keep your promise when it does. Afterwards, name what worked: “You sang a song and the time went quickly.”

visual.caption: Does it help you wait? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Hide the sweets in a box

lab.caption: Flagship lab: one biscuit now or two later, hide the treat, find the tricks that help, ask kindly, sort waits from get help now.

kid: Waiting is hard! You want the treat now. Patience means you can wait without a big fuss.
Waiting can be worth it. One biscuit now, or two biscuits after the timer? If you wait, you get more.

Some tricks help you wait. Put the treat where you cannot see it. Sing a song. Play with a toy. Count to 20. Take slow breaths. Looking at the treat, poking it, or asking “Is it time?” over and over makes it harder.
You can still ask, kindly: “Can I go next, please?” Then wait. But some things should not wait. If you are hurt, sick or scared, tell a grown-up right away.
adult: Ages 5 to 7. This is part of self-management in the IB PYP Personal, Social and Physical Education strand. It is also part of the self-regulation goals in early years and Key Stage 1. The aim: wait for a turn, a treat or help without getting very upset. Key terms: delayed gratification, self-regulation, impulse control, distraction.

The lab draws on Walter Mischel’s delay studies from the 1970s, often called the marshmallow test. Children waited much longer when the treat was covered or out of sight. They also waited longer when they kept busy, for example by singing or playing, than when they looked at the treat. Later work by Kidd, Palmeri and Aslin (2013) found that children waited far longer when an adult had kept an earlier promise. So waiting is partly a sensible choice about whether the promise is real. Larger studies since (Watts, Duncan and Quan, 2018) found the link between waiting at age 4 and later life is much smaller than first thought. Treat waiting as a skill that grows with practice, not a fixed trait.

Common mistakes: saying just be patient without giving a child a way to do it; leaving the treat or screen in full view; making a wait with no clear end, which feels endless to a young child; breaking a promised reward, which teaches that waiting does not pay; and treating every need as something to wait for. Be careful to teach that pain, feeling ill, feeling unsafe or being hurt are never things to wait about.

In the lab your child chooses one biscuit now or two after a sand timer. They drag a cup over the biscuit and a tablet into a drawer, and a want meter falls. They tap the tricks that help, pick patient words in three scenes, and sort things that can wait from times to get help now. Each wrong choice gets a short reason.

practice.prompt: Kit is waiting for a cake to cool. What helps Kit wait?
choices: Go and play with a toy
Stand by the cake and stare
practice.hint: Which one takes Kit’s mind off the cake?
practice.explain: Playing keeps Kit busy, so the wait feels shorter. Staring and poking keep Kit thinking about the cake.

practice.prompt: You can have 1 sticker now, or wait and get {n} stickers. How many more stickers do you get if you wait?
practice.hint: Take away the 1 you could have had now.
practice.explain: {n} stickers after waiting, minus the 1 now, is {=n-1} more stickers.

practice.prompt: Ali is on the swing and you want a go. What is the patient thing to say?
choices: Get off, it is my turn!
Is it my go? My go? My go?
practice.hint: Ask once, kindly, and then wait.
practice.explain: Asking once, kindly, lets Ali know you are next. Shouting or asking again and again does not help.

practice.prompt: You sing a song that is 1 minute long while you wait. Dinner is in {n} minutes. How many songs can you sing?
practice.explain: Each song lasts 1 minute, so {n} minutes is {n} songs.

practice.prompt: Which one should you NOT wait for?
choices: You fell and your knee is bleeding
practice.hint: Which one means you are hurt?
practice.explain: If you are hurt, tell a grown-up straight away. Turns and dinner are things you can wait for.

pool.prompt: You are waiting for a sweet. Where is the best place for it?
choices: Out of sight, in a box
pool.hint: Is it easier to wait when you can see it?
pool.explain: When you cannot see it, you want it less, so waiting is easier.

pool.hint: Think about waiting for your turn.
pool.explain: Patience is waiting calmly for something you want. You can still ask, kindly.

pool.prompt: Mum is on the phone and you want to tell her something. What can you do?
choices: Put your hand on her arm and wait
pool.hint: Find the way that lets her finish.
pool.explain: A hand on her arm tells Mum you are waiting. She can finish, then listen to you.

pool.prompt: You count to 10 slowly, then again, and again. You count to 10 {n} times. How many numbers did you count?
pool.hint: Each time you count, you say 10 numbers.
pool.explain: {n} times 10 is {=10*n} numbers. Counting gives your mind a job while you wait.

pool.prompt: Asking “Is it time yet?” over and over makes the wait...
pool.hint: Does asking make the time move?
pool.explain: Asking again and again keeps your mind on the wait, so it feels longer. It does not make it come sooner.

pool.prompt: Someone is hurting you. Should you wait?
choices: No, tell a grown-up you trust now
pool.hint: Patience is for things that can wait.
pool.explain: Being hurt is never a wait time. Tell a grown-up you trust right away.

pool.prompt: Zoe waits for a sand timer that runs {n} times. Each time takes 1 minute. How many minutes does Zoe wait?
pool.hint: One minute each time it runs.
pool.explain: {n} runs of 1 minute is {n} minutes of waiting.

pool.hint: Which one helps your body feel calm?
pool.explain: Slow breaths calm your body. Licking the treat or watching the clock makes waiting harder.

pool.prompt: Why can waiting be worth it?
choices: You may get something better later
pool.hint: Think of one biscuit now or two later.
pool.explain: Waiting can be hard, but it can bring something better later, like two biscuits instead of one.
